analysis.one_liner: Gives Americans enforceable rights over their personal data and restricts how companies collect, share, and sell it.
analysis.headline: The bill died in committee at the end of 2024 with no committee vote and no floor vote, despite being sponsored jointly by the chair and top Democrat of the committee that would handle it.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would give every American the right to see, correct, delete, and export the personal data companies hold on them, and to opt out of targeted advertising. It would require companies to ask permission before collecting sensitive data like health records, genetic information, face scans, and precise location, and it would put new limits on data brokers that buy and sell people's information. It was written together by the Republican chair and the Democratic ranking member of the House committee in charge, but it never got a markup or a vote before the two-year Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary internet users and phone owners. The bill would let anyone request the data a company holds about them, get it deleted or corrected, and take it to a competitor. Companies would need clear, specific permission before collecting health information, genetic data, biometrics like face or voice prints, precise location, or data about kids and teens, and refusing could not be harder than agreeing. Data brokers that profit by trading in people's information would face the tightest rules, and the FTC and state attorneys general could enforce the law.

how_it_helps.text: Every individual gets rights to access, correct, delete, and export the data companies hold, with large data holders and data brokers required to respond within 30 days.

Companies may only collect data that is necessary for the service a person asked for, and must get affirmative express consent before collecting or transferring sensitive data such as health, genetic, biometric, and precise location information.
Individuals can opt out of targeted advertising, and companies must make saying no at least as easy as saying yes, with no more than one extra step.

Data brokers are specially defined and regulated, privacy policies must name every broker a company sells to, and the bill adds privacy protections for children under 13 and teens under 17, including deletion rights for content posted as a minor.
The FTC, state attorneys general, and private individuals can all sue to enforce the rights, and companies cannot force users to waive them or deny service to people who refuse.

analysis.who_pays: Companies whose business runs on collecting and monetizing personal data: online advertising networks, data brokers, and large social media platforms. They would face new consent requirements, data minimization limits, security duties, and FTC enforcement. Consumers could also see some of these compliance costs passed on, and advertisers would rely more on context and first-party data than on tracking people across the web.

drawbacks.text: The bill would preempt state privacy laws, which critics, including California officials, warned could leave residents of states with stronger protections, like California's, worse off than under current law.
The bill would terminate the FTC's ongoing rulemaking on commercial surveillance and data security, trading away a regulatory process already underway in exchange for the statutory framework.

A private right of action is limited to substantial privacy harms, defined as at least $10,000 in financial harm or specific physical or mental harms, which civil-rights-minded critics said would be too narrow for most people to use in court.
Businesses below the thresholds, and companies generally, would bear real compliance costs to build consent systems, respond to deletion requests, and rewrite privacy practices in ten languages.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core protections are strong and directly address something almost every American experiences: companies gathering and selling personal data with little control by the person it belongs to. The honest tradeoffs are real. Federal preemption could reduce protections in states that currently have stronger laws, the bill ends the FTC's existing surveillance rulemaking, and the private lawsuit right is narrow. Whether the package is a net win depends a lot on how the FTC writes its rules and enforces it. On balance, the rights created here are the kind consumers cannot get in any other single step.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee in June 2024, and with no markup and no floor vote ever scheduled, it expired when the Congress ended in January 2025.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on June 25, 2024, with bipartisan sponsorship from the House Energy and Commerce Committee's top two members, Cathy McMorris Rodgers and Frank Pallone, plus Gus Bilirakis and Jan Schakowsky.
The same day, it was referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce, and that was the only action it ever received.
No committee markup, committee vote, or floor vote ever took place, and the bill died when the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Data brokers, online advertisers, and large platforms that profit from personal data are better off, since no national privacy law restricts them, and small businesses avoided new compliance costs. Ordinary Americans gained nothing, because the rights the bill created never took effect.

sides.party_line_note: The bill's sponsor was the committee's Republican chair and its lead cosponsor the committee's Democratic ranking member, with cosponsors from both parties, yet only 3 members signed on total (2 of 216 House Democrats and 1 of 224 House Republicans), and no vote ever separated the parties.

industries.note: The bill defines data brokers, requires privacy policies to name each one a company sells to, and blocks transfers of sensitive data without explicit consent. Their revenue comes from trading in personal information people never agreed to sell.

Individuals could opt out of targeted advertising outright, and data collection would be limited to what is necessary for the service requested. That strikes at the cross-site tracking that funds much of the online ad industry.

industries.industry: Large social media and tech platforms
industries.note: They would face consent requirements, data minimization, and special duties as large data holders, but federal preemption of state laws would replace the state-by-state patchwork they dislike. On net, the targeted-advertising and tracking restrictions are the bigger cost.
Businesses under $40 million in revenue with limited data holdings are excluded from the bill entirely, sparing them compliance costs while larger competitors absorb the new rules.
